title: Manage the harvesting process of agricultural crops

lessons.title: Planning the harvest
lessons.html:
Harvest planning starts months ahead

Harvest is when a season's investment is turned into income, and it is often the most labour- and machinery-intensive period on the farm. Poor planning causes losses through late harvesting, breakdowns, shortages of pickers, transport delays and quality rejections.

Elements of a harvest plan

  1. Yield estimate per block from crop counts, sample weighing or yield history.
  2. Timing: expected maturity dates by block and cultivar.
  3. Labour: number of pickers or operators, recruitment, contracts, training, transport and accommodation.
  4. Machinery and equipment: combines, harvesters, trailers, bins, crates, ladders; service before the season and stock critical spares.
  5. Storage and handling: silo or bag capacity, packhouse throughput, cold rooms.
  6. Market and logistics: buyer delivery schedules, transport bookings, documentation.
  7. Budget: harvest cost per tonne or per carton in ZAR.

Capacity matching

The harvest chain is only as fast as its slowest link. If pickers can fill 2 000 crates a day but the packhouse can pack only 1 500, fruit waits and quality drops. Calculate daily capacity at each step and plan accordingly.

Pre-harvest checks

  • Confirm that all pre-harvest intervals for agrochemicals have passed, as stated on the label.
  • Check food safety requirements: clean containers, toilets and hand-washing facilities for workers, and hygiene training.
  • Inspect fields for hazards: holes, wasp nests, snakes, power lines in reach of machinery.

Write the plan down and share it with supervisors, so everyone knows targets, responsibilities and contingency plans for rain or breakdowns.

lessons.title: Determining maturity and harvesting correctly
lessons.html:
Picking at the right time and in the right way

Maturity indices

Harvest timing affects yield, quality and shelf life. Indicators differ by crop:

CropCommon maturity indicators
Maize, wheat, soybeansGrain moisture content, physiological maturity
CitrusJuice content, sugar:acid ratio, colour
Apples and pearsFirmness, starch test, sugar (Brix), colour
GrapesSugar (Brix), acidity, taste
AvocadosMoisture or dry matter content
VegetablesSize, colour, firmness by market spec

Buyers and export protocols often specify minimum maturity standards. Test samples from each block and harvest in the order blocks reach maturity.

Grain harvesting

Set the combine for crop and conditions (drum or rotor speed, concave clearance, fan and sieves) to minimise cracked grain and losses. Check losses behind the machine regularly. Harvest at a moisture that allows safe storage or plan for drying.

Hand harvesting of fruit and vegetables

  • Train pickers in correct picking technique, for example clipping citrus stems short so they do not puncture other fruit.
  • Handle gently: bruises appear later in the market.
  • Do not overfill crates or bins.
  • Harvest in cooler parts of the day where possible, keep harvested produce in shade and move it quickly to the packhouse or cold store.

Field hygiene

Produce must not touch the soil, containers must be clean, and workers must wash hands after using toilets. Sick workers with diarrhoea or infected wounds should not handle fresh produce.

lessons.title: Post-harvest handling, safety and evaluation
lessons.html:
Protecting quality after harvest

Post-harvest handling

  • Cooling: remove field heat quickly with forced-air or hydrocooling for perishables. Every hour at high temperature shortens shelf life.
  • Grading and packing to buyer specifications; keep packing records for traceability.
  • Storage: grain must be dry, cool and protected from insects and rodents; fruit stored at correct temperature and humidity.
  • Transport: refrigerated trucks for perishables, maintaining the cold chain.

Health and safety during harvest

Harvest brings many workers, long hours and machinery together. Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, the employer must manage these risks.

  • Combines and balers: never clear blockages with the engine running. Stop, disengage drives, remove the key and wait for parts to stop.
  • Keep people away from moving machinery and augers; keep guards in place.
  • Ladder safety: three points of contact, ladders on firm ground.
  • Provide drinking water, shade and rest breaks to prevent heat stress.
  • Fire risk in dry grain fields: carry fire extinguishers on machinery, keep firebreaks, ban smoking.
  • Grain silos and bins: never enter without a permit, harness and a standby person; flowing grain can engulf a person.
  • Transport workers only on vehicles designed for passengers.

Evaluating the harvest

After the season, compare actual yields, quality grades, losses and costs per tonne with the plan. Calculate pack-out percentages and reasons for rejections. Hold a debrief with supervisors and contractors to list what went well and what to improve.

Key points

  • Plan yield, labour, machinery, storage and logistics in advance.
  • Match capacity across the whole harvest chain.
  • Harvest at the right maturity and handle produce gently.
  • Remove field heat quickly and keep the cold chain.
  • Never clear machine blockages with the engine running; manage heat and fire risk.
